chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Safwan ibn Yahya from Abd Allah ibn Muskhan from Humran ibn A'yan said:

I entered upon Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), and he said to me, 'With what have you professed the Ihram?' I said, 'With Umrah.' He said to me, 'Did you not profess the Ihram with Hajj and intend the Tamattu' (Umrah followed by Hajj)? Then your Umrah becomes Kufi (independent) and your Hajj becomes Makki (independent). And if you had intended the Tamattu' and professed the Ihram with Hajj, your Umrah and your Hajj would both be Kufi. The explanation in this report is that we should assume he had professed the Ihram with the independent Umrah, not the one with which one enjoys (Tamattu'). And if it were the one with which one enjoys, his Hajj would not be Makki, but his Hajj and his Umrah would both be Kufi, according to what he mentioned in his saying, 'And if you had intended the Tamattu'.' And it has also been narrated that if one professes the Ihram with Hajj as independent, it is permissible for him to make it an Umrah and enjoy with it until Hajj.

key_terms.الْمُتْعَةَ: Tamattu' (a type of Hajj where Umrah and Hajj are combined with a break)
key_terms.كُوفِيَّةً: Kufi (referring to the type of Hajj/Umrah associated with Kufa, implying a specific legal status or location of Ihram)
key_terms.مَكِّيَّةً: Makki (referring to the type of Hajj/Umrah associated with Mecca)
key_terms.يُتَمَتَّعُ: To enjoy (referring to the ritual of Tamattu')

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between independent Umrah and Umrah for Tamattu' in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) clarifies that the legal status of Hajj and Umrah depends on the initial intention (niyyah) at the Meeqat; entering with Umrah alone renders it independent (Mufradah), whereas entering with Hajj and intending Umrah first links them as Tamattu' (Kufiyyatan). This narration highlights the flexibility in Shia jurisprudence, noting that one may even convert an independent Hajj into an Umrah for Tamattu' if they initially professed Hajj, emphasizing the centrality of intention in ritual validity.
